strengths: DDOME addresses a useful problem: adapting to unseen federated clients without labeled test-time fine-tuning while transmitting only a subset of experts. The combination of client-level expert selection and per-sample routing is coherent, and Algorithm 1 and the loss definitions explain the intended protocol clearly.

The evaluation covers four classification datasets, two forms of label heterogeneity, and changing client populations. Reported accuracies—including 95.7% on CIFAR10, 78.6% on CIFAR100, and 74.9% on Yahoo! Answers—suggest practical promise within the studied settings.

The appendices provide useful ablations on common-expert quality, anchor sampling, expert initialization, and matched expert counts. Reporting failures with weaker common experts and insufficient anchoring is informative. The limitations and potential fairness risks are acknowledged candidly.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is false under the stated normalization. With x distributed as N(0, I_d/sqrt(d)), choose mutually orthogonal ground-truth router and expert subspaces, which the assumptions permit. Then E[y²] = 1/sqrt(d). Expert optimization cannot do worse than zero prediction, and subsequent router optimization cannot increase the optimal loss, so L(theta_hat) <= 1/(2 sqrt(d)), contradicting the claimed dimension-independent Ω(1) lower bound. Appendix J also changes the covariance to I_d/d and subsequently omits covariance factors. Separately, its application of Lemma 1 to span(V, V*) is unjustified: this span contains the fixed ground-truth router subspace, which may coincide with the expert subspace. These require substantive proof repairs.

The central claim that joint training is necessary for emergent specialization exceeds the evidence. Even a corrected theorem would address only one particular expert-first, router-second procedure, rather than establish a general necessity result. Experiments do not directly compare joint training with controlled frozen-router or sequential-training alternatives. Moreover, the main anchor construction explicitly partitions labels, assigns experts, and supervises the router with expert identities. The overlapping-label Dirichlet experiment is useful, but does not establish that specialization arises from implicit heterogeneity independently of this guidance.

The strongest performance claims need better-controlled baseline optimization. For example, the 93% CIFAR10 common expert falls to 58.4% with FedAvg and 71.4% with FedProx, whereas DDOME reaches 95.7%. Thus, the headline approximately 24-point advantage largely reflects baseline deterioration; improvement over retaining the available common expert is 2.7 points. Appendix B itself identifies learning-rate inconsistency as one cause of deterioration, and text experiments give DDOME a different optimizer and decay schedule. Comparable tuning protocols and a classifier trained on the same frozen embeddings would make the gains more convincing.

Originality relative to mixture-based personalized federated learning is insufficiently established. Joint router-expert optimization is longstanding in MoEs, and methods such as FedEM already address clients containing mixtures of shared latent distributions. Appendix I's k-means visualization does not substantiate its broad dismissal of clustering or mixture approaches. The distinctive contribution of anchor-guided sparse dispatch should be positioned more precisely against this literature.

Important reproducibility details are missing, particularly the common-expert pretraining data and recipe, checkpoint-selection procedure, gating-network dimensions, and baseline tuning settings. These matter because the ablations show sharp sensitivity to common-expert quality. Main tables provide no run counts or uncertainty estimates, and several appendix tables report the best test accuracy during training without explaining an independent validation protocol. No implementation or checkpoint release is identified in the manuscript.

The communication benefit of transmitting K rather than M experts is structurally plausible, but broader efficiency claims lack quantitative accounting. There are no complete communication-volume, inference-latency, or memory comparisons incorporating the common encoder, routing, and expert storage. Test-time prediction still requires common-encoder computation before running the selected expert, so sparse expert activation alone does not establish an end-to-end inference advantage.
